direct_claims: This chart compares pig production systems by two outcomes: greenhouse gas emissions per kilogram of deadweight and a welfare cost score.
It belongs to the domain of livestock production, environmental impact, and animal welfare assessment.
The title indicates the comparison is specifically for pig production.
The subtitle states that welfare cost is based on the quantity of years lived weighted by quality-of-life scores from detailed welfare assessments.
The subtitle also explains that a positive welfare cost means a cost to animal welfare, while a negative value indicates benefits to welfare.
The note states that the chart is based on 91 pig production systems across the United Kingdom and Brazil, with one dot representing one system.
The source is identified as Harriet Bartlett et al. (2024), and the chart is published by Our World in Data.
The plotted systems appear to cover several housing or production types, including outdoor, slatted, slatted plus straw yard, solid floor, straw yard, and straw yard plus outdoor.
In this chart, greenhouse gas emissions per kilogram deadweight represent the climate impact associated with producing a unit of pig meat output.
The welfare metric is not a direct measure of productivity or profit; it is an ethical assessment of animal well-being over the animals' lives.
Because negative welfare cost values indicate welfare benefits, systems farther left on the x-axis are better for animal welfare than systems farther right.
Systems lower on the y-axis have lower emissions intensity than systems higher on the y-axis.
The presence of multiple production categories suggests that housing and management choices are relevant factors in both emissions and welfare outcomes.
The note beneath the chart explicitly frames the issue as trade-offs in the externalities of pig production.
The inclusion of systems from both the United Kingdom and Brazil means the dataset spans more than one national production context.
